I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

There is something wrong with me as a person
I acted in ways that go against who I am

vignette:
Bao had been a journalist for fifteen years, a career built on bearing witness. It was on an assignment eighteen months ago, documenting a nascent political conflict, that he stopped being a witness and became a subject. Detained by a paramilitary faction, he was held for weeks in a windowless room. The interrogations were a blur of disorientation and fear; they would spin him in a chair until the world dissolved into a nauseating vortex, the dizziness a prelude to questions he couldn't answer. To break him, they played recordings through a speaker in his cell—a loop of harrowing sounds, the one that broke through his defenses most effectively being the high, desperate wail of a child crying. He was forced to name colleagues, to sign false confessions, to do things that felt like a betrayal of his very core. He was eventually released, but the man who came home was a fractured version of the one who had left.

In the first few months, the world felt like a minefield. The sound of children playing in the park across from his apartment, once a pleasant backdrop to his writing, now sent a jolt of raw fear through him. Hearing a name even vaguely similar to one of his captors would make his heart pound. This constant sense of ambient threat was exhausting. He found himself scanning the faces of strangers on the subway, convinced he could see malice in their eyes, watching them closely for any sign they might wish him harm. This state of high alert seemed to hold the trauma just below the surface, and on days when the threat felt most acute, the memories were hardest to keep at bay, surfacing as unwelcome sensory flashes. He would jump at the sound of a car backfiring or a door slamming shut. Feeling this afraid all the time, in response to such ordinary events, quietly confirmed the terrifying thought he was trying to resist: that this was simply who he was now, a person for whom the world was no longer safe. The memories of his captivity were not a coherent narrative he could recount; instead, they were intrusive fragments—the feeling of cold concrete on his cheek, the metallic taste of fear, the echo of that crying. To keep these fragments from ambushing him, he started to ruminate for hours, pacing his apartment while dissecting every decision that led him to that assignment in a desperate attempt to mentally undo what had happened. After these sensory fragments surfaced, his world felt primed for danger; the mental echo of the crying made the sound of actual children playing in the park feel like an imminent warning he could not afford to ignore. When he tried to deliberately recall the sequence of events, he found he couldn't; there were huge gaps, and the parts he could remember felt so extreme, so nightmarish, that it was hard to believe they had actually happened to him.

This fragmentation terrified him, cementing a belief that had taken root in that cell: there was something fundamentally wrong with him now, something permanently broken. The conviction that he was permanently changed kept pulling his mind back to the moments of his captivity, as if replaying the fragments of sensory horror was the only way to make sense of the damage that had been done. He felt exposed, as if his shame and weakness were visible to everyone he met, a stain they could see just by looking at him. This belief that he was inherently damaged made the world feel profoundly unsafe; if his weakness was on display, he was certain others would see it and seek to harm him. This deep-seated conviction that he was defective drove him inward. His certainty that he was now too fragile to cope with the world meant that things he once would have ignored—the sound of a child’s cry from the street, a name spoken in passing—now snagged his attention, holding the weight of a potential threat. He began to avoid the people he used to socialize with, especially old colleagues who knew the "before" Bao. The thought of their pity, or worse, their judgment, was unbearable. This self-imposed isolation, meant to keep him safe, instead created a quiet space where his triggers became magnified; the silence of his apartment made the sound of a child's cry from the street below feel impossibly loud and immediate. This isolation fed his hypervigilance; alone in his apartment, every creak of the building became a potential threat. The intense negative emotions—waves of horror, guilt over the things he’d said, and a profound, abiding shame—would become so overwhelming that he would stop eating, the emptiness in his stomach a dull, physical distraction from the chaos in his mind.

The cycle has only tightened its grip over the last year. A wave of dizziness from standing up too quickly, a consequence of his sporadic eating, is no longer just a physical sensation; it is an immediate somatic trigger that plunges him back into the disorienting helplessness of interrogation. This spike of fear makes him more attuned to other triggers, making the sound of a child’s cry from the street below feel like a direct assault. The sound brings not a clear memory but a sensory flash of dread and the powerful, unreal feeling of the events, which in turn amplifies his belief that he is losing his mind. He spends hours ruminating, pacing his apartment, dissecting every decision that led him to that assignment, a desperate attempt to mentally undo what happened. But this rumination only keeps the trauma fresh, sensitizing him further. His world has shrunk to his desk, where his editor, concerned by his refusal to leave his apartment for interviews, has relegated him to editing copy—a quiet demotion that feels like yet another confirmation of his own defectiveness. His marriage ended six months ago.

Bao finally sought therapy after a video call with his sister. Her son, his nephew, had started crying in the background, a normal toddler tantrum. Bao was seized by such a violent wave of horror and shame that he abruptly hung up without a word. The brief, shocked hurt on his sister’s face before the screen went dark was the catalyst. He came to the first session quiet and guarded, explaining that he felt he was becoming a ghost in his own life. What he fears most is that this broken, fearful man is not a temporary state, but the person he now is, permanently.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette does not state that Bao's negative beliefs about himself (e.g., being broken) cause or increase his sense of threat.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not state that Bao's negative appraisals of himself or the world cause his intrusive memories to surface.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not state that Bao's negative beliefs about himself make him more sensitive or attuned to triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not state that experiencing an intrusive memory makes Bao more sensitive or attuned to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not state that Bao's general sense of threat causes his intrusive memories to occur.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not state that feeling a sense of threat reinforces Bao's negative beliefs about himself being broken or defective.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
